```{python}
#| label: setup
#| output: false
# Every number and figure on this page is read from the stored results in
# data/02-analysis_data. No language model is called when the page is built.
import importlib.util
from pathlib import Path

import polars as pl
from IPython.display import HTML, display

ROOT = Path("..")


def load_script(name, file):
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(name, ROOT / "scripts" / file)
    module = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    spec.loader.exec_module(module)
    return module


si = load_script("si", "08-silicon_views.py")
query = load_script("query", "03-query_models.py")
sd = si.load(ROOT)
summary, seats = sd["summary"], sd["seats"]
ctrl = si.control_stats(seats)
rep_favoured = int((summary["p_rep_win"] >= 0.5).sum())
costs = si.cost_table(sd["resp"])
ind_shares = si.independents_shares(sd)
cmp = si.compare_with_regression(summary, ROOT)
n_agree = int((cmp["call"] != "Methods disagree").sum())
bt_stats = sd["bt"].group_by("model").agg(
    bias=pl.col("error").mean() * 100, mae=pl.col("error").abs().mean() * 100, right=pl.col("winner_right").sum()
)
calib = {r["model"]: r for r in sd["calib"].iter_rows(named=True)}

# Seat-chart numbers for the text (Figure 1)
import re

import numpy as np

rep_seats = seats["rep_seats"]


def pct(x, digits=0):
    return f"{100 * x:.{digits}f}%"


pct_dem = pct((rep_seats < si.MAJORITY_REP).mean())  # Democrats control
pct_tie = pct((rep_seats == 50).mean(), 1)  # exact 50-50 tie
pct_51 = pct((rep_seats == 51).mean(), 1)
pct_52 = pct((rep_seats == 52).mean(), 1)
pct_53 = pct((rep_seats == 53).mean(), 1)
pct_outright = pct((rep_seats >= 51).mean())  # control without the tie-break
pct_hold = pct((rep_seats >= 53).mean())  # hold or gain (53 today)
pct_gain = pct((rep_seats >= 54).mean())  # gain seats
pct_tails = pct(((rep_seats < 44) | (rep_seats > 60)).mean())
seat_min, seat_max = int(rep_seats.min()), int(rep_seats.max())
n_personas_26 = pl.read_parquet(ROOT / "data" / "02-analysis_data" / "personas_2026.parquet").height
personas_per_state = round(n_personas_26 / 35)

# National error: the assumed value set in 04-forecast.py
nat_sd = 100 * float(re.search(r"NATIONAL_SD = ([0-9.]+)", (ROOT / "scripts" / "04-forecast.py").read_text()).group(1))

# State error: leave-one-out error of the 2024 calibration line (as in 04-forecast.py)
loo = []
for m in sd["bt"]["model"].unique():
    d = sd["bt"].filter(pl.col("model") == m)
    x, y = d["rep_share"].to_numpy(), d["actual"].to_numpy()
    for i in range(len(x)):
        keep = np.arange(len(x)) != i
        b, a = np.polyfit(x[keep], y[keep], 1)
        loo.append(y[i] - (a + b * x[i]))
state_sd = 100 * float(np.std(loo, ddof=1))

# Corrected 2024 accuracy per model, leave-one-out (each state predicted by a line fitted without it)
loo_mae, loo_right = {}, {}
for m in ["GPT-4o mini", "Llama 3.3 70B"]:
    d = sd["bt"].filter(pl.col("model") == m)
    x, y = d["rep_share"].to_numpy(), d["actual"].to_numpy()
    preds = []
    for i in range(len(x)):
        keep = np.arange(len(x)) != i
        b, a = np.polyfit(x[keep], y[keep], 1)
        preds.append(a + b * x[i])
    preds = np.array(preds)
    loo_mae[m] = 100 * float(np.abs(y - preds).mean())
    loo_right[m] = int(((preds > 0.5) == (y > 0.5)).sum())

# Raw 2024 lean (actual - synthetic, points) split by which side won the race
lean_by_side = (
    sd["bt"].with_columns(side=pl.when(pl.col("actual") < 0.5).then(pl.lit("D")).otherwise(pl.lit("R")))
    .group_by("model", "side").agg(lean=(pl.col("actual") - pl.col("rep_share")).mean() * 100, n=pl.len())
)
lean = {(r["model"], r["side"]): r["lean"] for r in lean_by_side.iter_rows(named=True)}
n_dem_won = int(lean_by_side.filter(pl.col("side") == "D")["n"][0])
n_rep_won = int(lean_by_side.filter(pl.col("side") == "R")["n"][0])

# Person-level agreement in 2024 (Figure 4): unweighted share whose synthetic side matches their reported vote
PARTISAN = ["Strong Democrat", "Not Very Strong Democrat", "Lean Democrat",
            "Lean Republican", "Not Very Strong Republican", "Strong Republican"]  # fmt: skip
WHO = {"openai/gpt-4o-mini": "GPT-4o mini", "meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct": "Llama 3.3 70B",
       "party-line baseline": "Baseline"}  # fmt: skip
bp = sd["by_party"].filter(pl.col("model").is_in(list(WHO)))
part = bp.filter(pl.col("pid7").is_in(PARTISAN)).group_by("model").agg(
    agree=(pl.col("agreement") * pl.col("n")).sum() / pl.col("n").sum(), n=pl.col("n").sum()
)
agree_partisan = {WHO[r["model"]]: f"{100 * r['agree']:.1f}%" for r in part.iter_rows(named=True)}
n_partisan = {WHO[r["model"]]: f"{r['n']:,}" for r in part.iter_rows(named=True)}
ind = bp.filter(pl.col("pid7") == "Independent")
agree_ind = {WHO[r["model"]]: f"{100 * r['agreement']:.1f}%" for r in ind.iter_rows(named=True)}
n_ind_voted = int(ind["n"].max())  # pure independents with a reported vote for a major candidate
n_ind_rep = int(sd["personas_2024"].filter((pl.col("pid7") == "Independent") & (pl.col("voted_sen_party") == "Republican")).height)
n_ind_opp = n_ind_voted - n_ind_rep
pct_ind_rep = pct(n_ind_rep / n_ind_voted)


def share(df, source, side):
    row = df[(df["source"] == source) & (df["side"] == side)]
    return f"{100 * row['share'].iloc[0]:.0f}%" if len(row) else "0%"
```

On this page we forecast all 35 races held on November 3 in the 2026 U.S. Senate elections. For each of 5,173 real respondents from the 2024 Cooperative Election Study, we wrote a short persona, including information such as their age, gender, race, state, education, income, party identification, ideology. We then fed each persona in the first person to three large language models (the third for comparison only) and asked how the persona would vote. Each model gave 5 answers per persona. These answers were then weighted to midterm voters, corrected using a 2024 backtest, and used for 10,000 simulated elections. This method is called silicon sampling [@argyle2023]. We forecast a `{python} f"{100 * ctrl['p_rep_control']:.0f}%"` chance that Republicans keep control, with a median of `{python} f"{ctrl['median']:.0f}"` Republican seats  (80% interval `{python} f"{ctrl['lo']:.0f}"` to `{python} f"{ctrl['hi']:.0f}"`), and favored in `{python} str(rep_favoured)` out of 35 races.

## The forecast {#forecast}

```{python}
#| label: fig-seats
#| fig-cap: "Republican seats after the 2026 election in 10,000 simulated elections. Bars at 50 or more (red) are simulations in which Republicans keep control; the Vice President breaks a 50-50 tie. 31 Republican seats are not up this year and are counted in every simulation."
si.fig_seats(seats)
```

One full simulated election means that every one of the 35 races has a winner. We ran 10,000 of these simulated elections, and each one of them finished with a set number of Republican senators (31 Republican seats not up this year + races won by Republicans this year out of the 35). Each bar is one seat count (`{python} seat_min` to `{python} seat_max`). There is a total of 100 senate seats, and each bar counts simulations that ends with that number of Republican seats out of 100. So red bars are 50 or more Republican seats (Republicans control the senate), and blue bars are 49 or fewer (Democrats control the senate). If we add up all the red bars, we get `{python} f"{100 * ctrl['p_rep_control']:.0f}%"` of our simulations, meaning that republicans keep control of the senate in approximately 7/10 simulations.

The most common outcomes are `{python} f"{ctrl['median']:.0f}"` Republican seats (`{python} pct_52` of the simulations, also happens to be the median), 51 or 53 Republican seats (each `{python} pct_51` of the simulations), and an exact 50-50 tie (`{python} pct_tie` of the simulations). Republicans controlled the senate outright (51 or more seats) in `{python} pct_outright` of the simulations. Republicans gained more seats compared to today (54 or more seats) in `{python} pct_gain` of the simulations.

Notice that the spread of the histogram is very wide. The 80% interval is from `{python} f"{ctrl['lo']:.0f}"` to `{python} f"{ctrl['hi']:.0f}"`, which means that about 8 out of every 10 simulations have Republicans hold between `{python} f"{ctrl['lo']:.0f}"` and `{python} f"{ctrl['hi']:.0f}"` seats. The full range is `{python} seat_min` to `{python} seat_max` seats. Why is our histogram so wide? For every simulated election we introduce four kinds of uncertainty. First is a national error shared by every state, where we draw one number from a normal distribution with a set standard deviation of `{python} f"{nat_sd:.0f}"` percentage points to determine how far the forecast is off nationwide. This matters because if state wise errors were independent, they would often cancel each other out and lead to a bunched-together histogram around `{python} f"{ctrl['median']:.0f}"`. Moving every state in the same direction is also honest because real polling misses also tend to run the same way across states, like in 2016 and 2020 [@gelman2020]. Second is a state error drawn for each separate race to capture local factors (effect of candidates, local issues, campaign success), it was measured as how far off the corrected forecast was for each state in the 2024 backtest and has a standard deviation of `{python} f"{state_sd:.1f}"` percentage points. Third, in each simulation we pick one of two LLM models (GPT-4o mini or Llama 3.3 70B) and use its numbers for every state. And fourth, there is sampling error caused by the limited number of personas for each state (about `{python} personas_per_state` on average).


```{python}
#| label: fig-states
#| fig-cap: "Forecast for each race. Each row shows 20 equally likely outcomes from the simulations [@kay2016]: the Republican's share of the vote against the main opposition (a Democrat, or an independent in Idaho, Montana, Nebraska and South Dakota). Red dots are simulated Republican wins, blue dots opposition wins. Rows are sorted by the median."
si.fig_state_dots(sd["draws"], summary)
```

In this graph, each row is 1 race/1 state, so there are 35 rows total. Looking at the 50% line, a dot to the right is a Republican win, and a dot to the left is an opposition win. There are 20 dots on each row, and each dot is one equally likely outcome. So, what is a dot and where does it come from? For each state, we sort the 10,000 simulated results from most Democratic to most Republican and then cut this sorted list into 20 equal slices each with 500 simulations. Each dot is the middle of one of these slices and stands for about a 5% chance. This graph is a quantile dot plot, used by @kay2016 because people are better at judging chances by counting outcomes rather than looking at a probability curve or reading a numerical percentage. So, to get a rough chance that Republicans win, just count the red dots (the dots to the right of the 50% line). Just keep in mind that counting is only accurate to about 5 percentage points, and you can refer to @tbl-forecast for exact chances.

Rows are sorted by median, so the most Republican races are at the top of the graph, and the most Democratic races are at the bottom. The closest races are the ones where the dots straddle 50%. The two closest races here are Texas and North Carolina, where there are 11 red dots out of 20, giving an approximate Republican chance of 55% (the actual exact chance is `{python} f"{100 * summary.filter(state='TX')['p_rep_win'][0]:.0f}%"`). Michigan has 13 red dots, with a Republican chance of `{python} f"{100 * summary.filter(state='MI')['p_rep_win'][0]:.0f}%"`, and is a seat that Republicans are favored to take from Democrats. Georgia has 7 red dots and a Republican chance of `{python} f"{100 * summary.filter(state='GA')['p_rep_win'][0]:.0f}%"`; it is a Democratic seat where Republicans are behind.


## How the forecast is built {#method}

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(si.pipeline_html())
```

First, we created personas. We used the 2024 respondents in the cumulative CES file, which sets every year’s survey into one consistent format [@kuriwaki2025]. We included only respondents who live in the 35 states with a 2026 senate race, and randomly drew up to 150 respondents in each state (A few had fewer respondents and the minimum is 95). This process gave us a total of `{python} n_personas_26` personas. A persona is a short paragraph written in first person, built from a real respondent’s own answers [@argyle2023], which in our case includes details regarding age, race, gender, state, education, family income, party identification (on a 7-point scale from strong Democrat to strong Republican), ideology (very liberal to very conservative), religious attendance, and how closely they follow politics. If a respondent left an answer blank, that detail is left entirely out of their persona. We use these 2024 respondents to stand in for 2026 voters because we did not survey anybody in 2026.

Second, we created prompts for the AI models. They contained in order: a system message telling the model to answer as the person using only knowledge about politics they would have, the persona, the ballot (in Ohio and Florida it says special election, in independent races it says, “an independent”, and in Montana and Mississippi it lists all three), and all allowed answers (Republican, Democrat, Other, Would not vote). We got the 2026 ballot from Wikipedia [@wiki2026]. Candidates are described only by their party and not their name in order to keep 2024 and 2026 comparable. See [the example prompt below](#ohio-prompt). For pure independents, the models mostly answered “Other” even though in 2024 about half of the self-reported independents picked either Democrat or Republican. We remedied this with a follow-up question forcing a choice, which is detailed further in [The independents problem](#independents).

Third, we used 3 models through OpenRouter [@citeOpenRouter]. We used GPT-4o mini [@gpt4omini] and Llama 3.3 70B [@llama33] for our forecasting because their training data ends before the 2024 election, allowing them to be tested on 2024. We used DeepSeek V4 Flash [@deepseekv4] for comparison only because its knowledge on 2025-26 means it cannot be tested on 2024. Each model gave five answers for every persona. We used temperature 1, so answers are sampled in proportion to how likely the model thinks each asnwer is. For example, a persona responding Republican 3/5 times is counted as 60% Republican rather than as 1 Republican vote. Our number of replies and total cost are detailed below in @tbl-costs.

Fourth, we produced state estimates from our answers through weights. Each persona gets a Republican share, which is Republican answers divided by answers for any major candidate on the ballot (Republican, Democrat, independent). In the three-way races in Montana and Mississippi, we measure Republican against the Democrat and independent combined. Each persona’s weight is calculated by their CES survey weight (makes the sample match the state’s adult population) multiplied by their turnout probability (the share of 2022 CES respondents in the same age band, college/no college, and news-interest group who actually voted, according to official voter records). We conducted post-stratification, meaning the estimate of each state is the weighted average of the shares of its personas.

Fifth, we conducted calibration. In our 2024 backtest with 33 races and 4,833 personas, the raw estimates were too Democratic and extreme, which @bisbee2024 also recognized. For each model we fit a straight line on the 33 races, `actual = a + b × raw`. For GPT the slope was `{python} f"{calib['GPT-4o mini']['slope']:.2f}"`, and for Llama the slope was `{python} f"{calib['Llama 3.3 70B']['slope']:.2f}"`. A slope of about 0.63 says that the real results are about 2/3 as lopsided as the synthetic results. Our line corrects every 2026 estimate since the intercept corrects the Democratic lean and the slope pulls extreme estimates toward the middle. We conducted this calibration with the assumption that the 2024 model errors carry over to 2026.

Lastly, we simulated 10,000 elections. In each election we add random errors to every state’s corrected estimate, and the state is called for the candidate with above 50%. The number of Republican seats is counted, and we add the 31 Republican seats that are not up. The four sources of uncertainty are detailed in the explanation of @fig-seats.

```{python}

races26 = {r["state"]: r for r in sd["races_2026"].iter_rows(named=True)}
example = pl.read_parquet(ROOT / "data" / "02-analysis_data" / "personas_2026.parquet").filter(
    pl.col("state") == "OH"
).sample(1, seed=853).row(0, named=True)
prompt = query.build_prompt(example["backstory"], races26["OH"], 2026)
print(f'<div class="prompt-box"><b>System:</b> {query.SYSTEM_PROMPT}\n\n<b>User:</b> {prompt}</div>')
```

This persona, drawn at random, is real and made from a CES 2024 respondent from Ohio. The prompt is shown in the exact form it is fed to the models. Note that this persona is a pure independent, which is the type of persona that led models to answer “Other”, and receive a follow-up calling it to choose between the Republican and Democratic candidate, as described in [the independents problem](#independents).

## Does it work? The 2024 backtest {#backtest}

What is our backtest? We ran the same pipeline as described in the [method section](#method), but on the 2024 Senate races which already have known results. Here we had 4,833 personas in 33 races, and weights were `survey weight × each person’s validated 2024 turnout`. We compared the synthetic Republican share from each state with its actual 2024 result from @wiki2024. It is from this test that we got our calibration line and `{python} f"{state_sd:.1f}"`-point state error used to forecast 2026.

Before any correction, the average lean (actual – synthetic) was +`{python} f"{bt_stats.filter(model='GPT-4o mini')['bias'][0]:.1f}"` points for GPT and +`{python} f"{bt_stats.filter(model='Llama 3.3 70B')['bias'][0]:.1f}"` points for Llama, meaning that real results were more Republican. The average miss was `{python} f"{bt_stats.filter(model='GPT-4o mini')['mae'][0]:.1f}"` points for GPT and `{python} f"{bt_stats.filter(model='Llama 3.3 70B')['mae'][0]:.1f}"` points for Llama. Both models called `{python} str(bt_stats.filter(model='GPT-4o mini')['right'][0])` out of 33 races correctly. Synthetic voters were too Democratic by an average of `{python} f"{lean[('GPT-4o mini', 'D')]:.1f}"` points (GPT) and `{python} f"{lean[('Llama 3.3 70B', 'D')]:.1f}"` points (Llama) in the `{python} str(n_dem_won)` races that Democrats won. Synthetic voters were too Republican by a smaller average of `{python} f"{abs(lean[('GPT-4o mini', 'R')]):.1f}"` (GPT)  and `{python} f"{abs(lean[('Llama 3.3 70B', 'R')]):.1f}"` (Llama) in the `{python} str(n_rep_won)` races Republicans won. This matches @bisbee2024, where synthetic samples show too little variation and exaggerate difference between groups. In @fig-backtest below, the solid calibration line being flatter than the dashed line visualizes this “too extreme”. The wrong calls were mostly very close races. Both models incorrectly called Nevada, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, and Ohio, which were all races that were decided by just a few points in 2024. After correction, GPT’s average miss fell to `{python} f"{loo_mae['GPT-4o mini']:.1f}"` points, and Llama’s fell to `{python} f"{loo_mae['Llama 3.3 70B']:.1f}"` points. GPT called `{python} str(loo_right['GPT-4o mini'])` races, but Llama correctly called `{python} str(loo_right['Llama 3.3 70B'])` still. We used leave-one-out to fit a line without the state being predicted, because partly fitting a line to the state being predicted may lead us to overestimate the improvement.


```{python}
#| label: fig-backtest
#| fig-cap: "2024 backtest. Each dot is one of the 33 Senate races of 2024: the synthetic voters' Republican share (before calibration) against the actual result [@wiki2024]. The dashed line is a perfect forecast; the solid line is the calibration line fitted to these races and used to correct the 2026 forecast. The three largest misses for each model are labeled."
si.fig_backtest(sd["bt"], sd["calib"])
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-agreement
#| fig-cap: "Person by person in 2024: the share of synthetic voters who pick the same side (Republican or opposition) as the real respondent reported voting, by party identification. The party-line baseline simply has everyone vote with their party, so it has no prediction for pure independents."
si.fig_by_party(sd["by_party"])
```

Did each synthetic voter pick the same side as the real person? For each persona and each model, we first determine which side (Republican or opposition) won the majority of the five answers from the model and then check whether the real person also voted for the same side. For pure independents, we score them on the forced-choice answers. The score is the share of people where the two votes agree. We compare against a party-line baseline, which means that everybody just votes for their party. Note that pure independents don’t have a score for this baseline, so the overall comparison leaves out pure independents and people who are “not sure”.

For our ~3,060 partisans, the models performed no better than the party-line baseline. GPT had an agreement of `{python} agree_partisan['GPT-4o mini']`, Llama had an agreement of `{python} agree_partisan['Llama 3.3 70B']`, and the party-line baseline had an agreement of `{python} agree_partisan['Baseline']`. This suggests that the models add little to nothing beyond the voter’s party when it is known. For pure independents, the agreements were much lower, with `{python} agree_ind['GPT-4o mini']` for GPT and `{python} agree_ind['Llama 3.3 70B']` for Llama. In reality, `{python} n_ind_rep` pure independents responded that they voted Republican and `{python} n_ind_opp` for the opposition. Just guessing Republican would be correct about `{python} pct_ind_rep` of time. The approximate 65% from the models do better than this, but still perform much worse for either partisan group. @argyle2023 also found that when matching real voters, their silicon samples performed much better for partisans than for independents. This is likely because the persona has no “party-to-vote-for” information, which we think gives a lot of the forecast signal for partisans. See @fig-agreement above, where each marker is close together in partisan rows, and the pure independent row has its markers further to the left and has no baseline marker.

## Uncertainty, costs and limits {#limits}

```{python}
#| label: tbl-costs
#| tbl-cap: "Every model call made for this project, through OpenRouter. The first 2026 run is included although DeepSeek's answers from it were unusable (its reasoning used up the reply limit) and were replaced by the rerun. When: the date and the times of the first and last call of each run in 2026, Toronto time."
display(HTML(si.booktabs(costs, ["Models", "Replies", "Cost (US$)"])))
```

::: {.write}
Discussion, connecting to the literature:
@argyle2023 (algorithmic fidelity; independents), @bisbee2024 (too little variance, exaggerated differences: our slope
of about 0.63), @heath2026 (mode collapse; our "Other" answers), @gelman2020 (correlated errors, the national swing as
an assumption, rounding probabilities).
Limits: one calibration election, from a presidential year; the 3-point national swing is assumed; candidates are
described by party only; no 2026 survey; three-way races (Maine 2024, Montana and Mississippi 2026) are measured
against the combined opposition. Where the forecast disagrees with expert ratings (Massachusetts, Illinois, Michigan,
Ohio, Nebraska, Alaska) and why. Total cost: US$`{python} f"{costs.attrs['total_cost']:.2f}"`.
:::

## Appendix: the full forecast {#appendix}

```{python}
#| label: tbl-forecast
#| tbl-cap: "Forecast for all 35 races of 2026, sorted by the Republican's chance of winning. Median and 80% interval are the Republican share of the vote against the main opposition across 10,000 simulations; (I) marks an independent main opponent. display(HTML(si.booktabs(si.forecast_table(summary, sd["races_2026"]), ["Median R share", "80% interval", "P(Republican wins)"])))
```

## Software and data {.unnumbered}

Analysis in Python [@citePython] with uv [@citeUv], Polars [@citePolars], pandas [@citePandas], NumPy [@citeNumpy],
PyArrow [@citeArrow], scikit-learn [@citeScikit], plotnine [@citePlotnine] and Matplotlib [@citeMatplotlib]; site
built with Quarto [@citeQuarto] and set in Newsreader [@newsreader]. Models: GPT-4o mini [@gpt4omini], Llama 3.3 70B
[@llama33] and DeepSeek V4 Flash [@deepseekv4] through OpenRouter [@citeOpenRouter]. Survey data from the Cumulative CES
[@kuriwaki2025]; candidates and results from @wiki2026 and @wiki2024.
